active_themes.label: Warsh Into the Headwind
active_themes.summary: Warsh's measured-cuts narrative relied on a falling oil trajectory and stable consumer spending. Today's 3.4% inflation print broke the first assumption: oil has already driven inflation to three-year highs despite de-escalation talk. The second assumption—stable spending—is untested until May 29. Warsh has not yet publicly acknowledged that energy inflation, not transitory demand, is the constraint, and that's a strategic silence that will not survive another week. If May 29 spending is weak, Warsh will have cut into demand destruction and will face immediate market pressure to pause. If spending holds, he keeps the narrative intact—for now.

active_themes.label: Iran Deal Credibility Test
active_themes.summary: Iran state TV reports of a draft deal that would reopen Hormuz and end naval blockade drove oil down from $92+ to near $88, the first de-escalation signal in weeks. But today's inflation print—3.4% PCE, a three-year high—reveals the market's core assumption was wrong: even with deal rumors, oil stayed elevated long enough to push headline inflation to crisis levels. The question is no longer whether a deal happens; it's whether the oil spike has already done enough damage to consumer balance sheets that the deal, even if it closes, arrives too late to prevent credit tightening cascades. Watch for deal collapse signals (next 48 hours) or concrete Hormuz reopening timelines (next week). If talks collapse, oil re-spikes above $95 and forces Warsh into a policy bind: cut into 4%+ inflation or hold into tightening credit.

active_themes.label: Lenders' Early Exit Confirmed
active_themes.summary: No major lender announcement today, but the silence is deafening. Banks have already begun quietly withdrawing from the deposit and consumer credit markets before Warsh's rate cuts compress yields and trigger depositor flight. The mechanism is locked in. Today's inflation print—a three-year high—validates their thesis: spending must weaken soon, and pulling early is rational. May 29 spending data will either confirm their pessimism (weak spending validates early withdrawal, equities capitulate) or expose it as over-tightening (spending holds, credit reverses, equities rally hard). This is the highest-stakes binary for the next 72 hours.

active_themes.label: May 29: The System Test
active_themes.summary: Nasdaq +0.91% reflects relief on the (still-fragile) assumption that an Iran deal will ease energy inflation and allow Warsh to cut without demand destruction. Dow +0.05% reflects the market's actual belief: broad equities are skeptical consumers can hold up. May 29 April spending data (released Friday morning) will test which thesis is right. If spending shows MoM decline or 0% change, lenders' pre-emptive tightening was rational, institutional withdrawal accelerates, and equities face a 3-5% correction. If spending posts +0.4% or higher, lenders over-tightened, credit reverses, and equities gap up 2-3% on the realization that soft landing is still possible.

active_themes.label: Long Duration Repricing Locked In
active_themes.summary: The 30-year yield is at 2007 highs; institutional consensus is already priced that Warsh's cuts weaken the dollar, push oil higher, and force long-duration repricing as inflation expectations reset. No new development today, but today's mixed equity action confirms the consensus is holding: the bond market and the broad equity market agree that cuts into $90+ oil and tightening credit is a negative trade-off, not a healing scenario. Today's Nasdaq relief on AI is a tactical relief, not a reframe of that structural view.
